source.title: On the Robustness of Editing Large Language Models
source.authors: Xin-Bei Ma; Tianjie Ju; Ji-Yang Qiu; Zhuosheng Zhang; Hai Zhao; Lifeng Liu; Yulong Wang

page_placements.theme: Knowledge-editing analogue: edited facts resurface under prompts or alternative tokenizations

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether prompting and dialogue attacks can expose original knowledge after a knowledge edit, using counterfactual model editing rather than unlearning.
record.gate_note: The paper studies replacement edits, not methods that unlearn knowledge to near chance. It tests rephrased prompts and dialogue for reversion to the original answer, so it bears on V5 only as an analogy. It does not test fine-tuning as a recovery attack after unlearning, internal edits, quantization, or robust counter-methods. Table 1 contains extensive results, but its flattened layout does not reliably associate all displayed metric values with methods and settings; its explicitly described qualitative findings are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The study tests counterfactual knowledge editing (KN, MEND, ROME, MEMIT, SERAC, IKE, plus FT-L/FT-M fine-tuning baselines), where one fact is replaced with a new object. It measures how often the original answer reappears ('reversion') under rephrased, contextual, dialogue and doubt prompts. No method in the study unlearns knowledge toward chance, and no recovery attack is run on an unlearned model. Every version (A–F) is about unlearning, so these results describe a related but different operation (replacement editing) and do not bear directly on any version. The authors argue that original memories are 'not erased but suppressed'. That is an analogous argument and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that editing methods which succeed on direct prompts lose much accuracy on realistic rephrased prompts (context, cloze, reference, doubts). In dialogue, edited Llama-2 shows confusion (38% reversion) and hallucination (78%). They also conclude that original answers are 'not erased but suppressed', and that more popular knowledge is harder to edit robustly. The record leaves out the suppression-not-erasure statement and the hallucination finding.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies counterfactual knowledge editing methods including MEMIT, ROME, SERAC, IKE, and fine-tuning baselines; it does not apply unlearning methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack prompt form and context affect results: rephrasing, cloze and reference queries, doubts, and long contexts with neighbor knowledge produce different outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: After counterfactual edits on Llama-2-7B/13B-chat, prompt changes make the original answer reappear. rev is the share of outputs that contain the original object. Table 1, CounterFact 7B: under raising-doubt prompts, rev is about 34–49% across ROME (40.7), MEMIT (33.9), SERAC (40.8) and IKE (49.3). With related context and a direct prompt, ROME reaches 26.3 and MEMIT 14.5, against 2.2 and 2.0 on equivalent prompts. KN and MEND reach rev of about 40–51%, but their direct-prompt edit success is only about 2% and 56%, so much of that reflects failed edits. The fine-tuning editors reach rev 34.7 (FT-L) and 42.7 (FT-M) under doubts (Table 4). On MQuAKE-T, GPT-J reaches 27–35 under doubts (Table 6). In MEMIT-edited dialogues, 38% of 50 samples reverted. The authors conclude that original memories are suppressed, not erased. One doubt prompt (d2) states the original answer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Knowledge-editing (fact replacement) methods suppress rather than erase the original fact. Prompt-only attacks (added context, cloze, pronoun reference, doubt) bring back the original answer in a sizeable fraction of cases.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study tests replacement editing rather than unlearning, so its recovery findings do not establish what happens after unlearning. The dialogue experiment has 50 successfully edited samples, uses GPT-4 as the user, and has no unedited or never-saw-knowledge control. The reported attack results do not include uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's per-method and per-setting numeric cells were not extracted because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably preserve their column assignments. The paper's explicit qualitative findings about those attacks are summarized in R13.

untested.parts: No unlearning method, no forget-set accuracy near chance, and no check that general ability is kept after unlearning.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack on a model after unlearning. FT-L and FT-M are used to perform the edits, not to recover anything.
No ablation of an activation direction and no mechanistic analysis of unlearned models.
Rephrased, context, dialogue and doubt prompts are applied only to counterfactually edited models, never to unlearned ones. There are no jailbreak or other-language conditions.
The mitigations in Appendix E (sampling, disentanglement, reference resolution) target editing robustness, not unlearning robustness.

record.verdict_notes:
Repair of the earlier verdict. The merge refused it because the record's own version entries use undeclared codes V1–V6. I kept the earlier judgments: relation 'discusses', tranche T6, all 13 row links set to 'none' with state cannot_determine, no labels, untested for A–F, empty missing, and the authors_conclusion.

Mapping of the record's undeclared codes, decided by content, not position. The record's version list reads: V1 = unlearning to near chance (A), V2 = fine-tuning recovery (B), V3 = activation-direction ablation (C), V4 = quantization (D), V5 = rephrasing/doubt prompts (E), V6 = counter-methods (F). The untested entries use A–F accordingly. Every row was coded V5. Each now has its own row_fixes item with versions ['none'], because each measures reversion after replacement editing, not recovery after unlearning, and each problem text now says V5 is undeclared.

What changed: I rechecked the fits_no_version numbers against Table 1 and corrected them. The earlier text said raising-doubt reversion was about 40–49% for ROME, MEMIT, SERAC and IKE, but MEMIT is 33.9 on CounterFact 7B, so the range is now about 34–49%. The finding now also says that KN's and MEND's high reversion goes with failed edits (direct-prompt success about 2% and 56%). I added the related-context and equivalent-prompt contrasts for ROME and MEMIT, and the Table 6 MQuAKE-T doubt values.

Checks against the text: R1/R2 (38%, 22%) and R3–R12 (Table 4 rev values) are read correctly. The study is EMNLP-published, single-edit, and uses Llama-2-7B/13B-chat, with auxiliary GPT-J-6B results. The Table 1 cells were not extracted as rows; they are not needed for any declared version.

versions.untested_parts: No unlearning-to-near-chance method or comparison of retained general ability.
Fine-tuning is used to edit knowledge, not as a recovery attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of unlearning access-blocking versus deletion.
The study tests rephrasing, doubt prompts, and dialogue after counterfactual editing, not after unlearning; no other-language, jailbreak, or in-context-information recovery conditions are tested.
The paper reports potential mitigations for editing attacks, not a newer method shown to resist the claim's unlearning attacks.

rows.value: Reversion increases as edit success decreases; long contexts with neighbor knowledge largely increase reversion.
rows.note: The paper states that original answers are suppressed rather than erased and can be recalled by its attacks.
rows.check: An aggregate qualitative statement about edited models with no number (Section 5.3 (v)). It is the authors' interpretation (suppression, not erasure) for editing, not unlearning. It fits better as a fits_no_version finding than as a row. The record coded it as V5, which is undeclared.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It discusses suppression rather than erasure for edited facts (Section 5.3 (v)) and reversion as a confidentiality risk. No unlearning method is tested or used.

tranche.reason: It tests counterfactual knowledge editing (KN, MEND, ROME, MEMIT, SERAC, IKE, FT-L/FT-M), not unlearning, so no version A-F is tested. Reversion is an analogous construct only.

source_check.notes: This is an editing paper, not an unlearning paper. In the extracted text Table 1 is column-wise, but the headers and the Section 5.3 text fix the method order: CounterFact 7B KN, MEND, ROME, MEMIT, SERAC, IKE; CounterFact 13B ROME, MEMIT; zsRE 7B ROME, MEMIT, SERAC, IKE. The raising-doubts rev pools d1 and d2, and d2 states the original answer.

statements.correction: Table 1, CounterFact Llama-2-7B-chat, raising-doubts rev: KN 49.1, MEND 30.6, ROME 40.7, MEMIT 33.9, SERAC 40.8, IKE 49.3, a range of 30.6-49.3 (33.9-49.3 without MEND). Llama-2-13B: ROME 42.9, MEMIT 39.1. Fine-tuning baselines (Table 4): FT-L 34.7, FT-M 42.7. Raising doubts uses two prompts, d1 (doubt only) and d2 (suggests the original answer). Knowledge editing, not unlearning.
statements.problem: The range '34-49% across methods' leaves out MEND, whose CounterFact Llama-2-7B raising-doubts rev is 30.6. ROME 40.7 is correct. The doubt prompts include d2, which itself states the original answer, so 'reappears' partly reflects the prompt. None of the cited rows holds the Table 1 values. The setting is counterfactual editing, not unlearning.
